> **What this case shows** — posturography, quantifying center-of-pressure (COP) sway during quiet
> standing, is a core balance and fall-risk assessment. Its standard metrics come from **Prieto et al.
> (1996)**. The ecosystem ships the full set in `swayMetrics` but had never checked it against the
> reference. This case certifies it: on a real 60-second quiet-standing trial, `PhysioMoCap::swayMetrics`
> reproduces an independent reimplementation of the Prieto formulas **bit-for-bit**, and the 95%
> confidence ellipse turns out to contain 96.7% of the COP samples — correctly calibrated.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — `swayMetrics(cop, sampling_rate)` → the full Prieto posturography metric set.
**Way of thinking** — the stabilogram (COP path) is summarized by a handful of numbers: how far it travels
(path length), how fast (mean velocity), and how much area it covers (95% ellipse). Compare them *between
conditions* (eyes open/closed, firm/foam) or *groups* (fallers vs non-fallers) — that is where they
discriminate.
**Ecosystem usage** — `PhysioMoCap::swayMetrics()`.
:::

## Proposition

On a real 60-s quiet-standing COP trial, `swayMetrics` reproduces an independent Python reimplementation
of the Prieto (1996) formulas bit-for-bit (path length 37.2 cm, mean velocity 0.62 cm/s, 95% ellipse
0.94 cm², sway area 0.046 cm²/s; max `|diff|` ~7e-13); the 95% confidence ellipse contains 96.7% of the
COP samples.

## Question & goal

**The question is a certification and a calibration check: the ecosystem ships the Prieto posturography
suite but had never tested it — do the metrics match the reference, and is the 95% ellipse correctly
scaled?** The goal is to certify `swayMetrics` bit-for-bit and confirm the ellipse construct.

## Challenge & approach

The Prieto metrics are deterministic closed forms of the COP trajectory: mean/RMS distance from the mean
COP, total excursion (path length), mean velocity, the 95% confidence circle and ellipse areas (from the
resultant-distance statistics and the COP covariance), and the sway area. We compute them with
`swayMetrics` and with an independent Python reimplementation of the Prieto formulas, and check what
fraction of COP samples lands inside the fitted 95% ellipse.

```
BDS quiet-standing COP (60 s, 100 Hz) → swayMetrics → path 37.2 cm · mvelo 0.62 cm/s · 95% ellipse 0.94 cm²
                                      vs independent Prieto reimplementation → max |diff| ~7e-13 (bit-for-bit)
                                      95% confidence ellipse contains 96.7% of the COP samples (calibrated)
```

## Data

**Santos & Duarte (2016) balance dataset (figshare)**: subject **1**, **eyes-open firm-surface** trial,
60 s of quiet standing on a force platform, COP sampled at 100 Hz (6000 samples). Details in
[`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![Left: the stabilogram — the COP sway path (blue) in the mediolateral × anteroposterior plane, with the fitted 95% confidence ellipse (red); 96.7% of the samples fall inside it. Right: the key Prieto metrics (path length /10, mean velocity, 95% ellipse and circle areas, sway area ×10), each reproducing the independent Prieto reimplementation bit-for-bit.](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* left — the stabilogram is the raw balance signal; the ellipse is the compact 95%
summary of where the COP lives. Right — every summary metric equals the reference to machine precision.

| Quantity | Value |
|---|--:|
| **path length** | **37.2 cm** |
| **mean velocity** | **0.62 cm/s** |
| **95% ellipse area** | **0.94 cm²** |
| 95% circle area | 0.95 cm² |
| sway area | 0.046 cm²/s |
| max \|diff\| vs Prieto | **~7e-13** (bit-for-bit) |
| samples inside the 95% ellipse | **96.7%** |

The full Prieto suite equals the reference exactly, and the ellipse is calibrated. Values trace to
[`artifacts/sway_summary.csv`](artifacts/sway_summary.csv).

## Conclusion

The ecosystem's `swayMetrics` is now certified against the canonical Prieto posturography formulas. The
transferable takeaway: **the stabilogram compresses to a few well-defined numbers — path length, mean
velocity, and the 95% ellipse area are the workhorses. Certifying that they are computed correctly is the
prerequisite for the comparisons that matter clinically: eyes-open vs eyes-closed, firm vs foam, faller
vs non-faller.**

## Open questions

- Posturography discriminates *between conditions and groups*, not within a single trial; the BDS
  dataset's four conditions (vision × surface) across 163 subjects support that population analysis. This
  single-trial certification establishes the metrics are computed correctly — the prerequisite for any
  such comparison. *Documented, not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

| Step | Function | Package |
|---|---|---|
| Posturography sway metrics | `swayMetrics()` | PhysioMoCap |
| Movement smoothness (SPARC / LDLJ) | `sparc()`, `ldlj()` | PhysioMoCap |

**Reading the result.**

- **path length / mean velocity** — larger = more sway (poorer steadiness); the most reliable, most-used
  measures.
- **95% ellipse area** — the compact spatial spread of the COP; compare across conditions, not as an
  absolute.

**The recipe, copy-runnable:**

```r
library(PhysioMoCap)

sm <- swayMetrics(cop, sampling_rate = 100)   # cop = 2-column (ML, AP) center of pressure
sm$path_length; sm$mean_velocity; sm$area_ce  # the workhorse metrics
# the Prieto metric set reproduces the reference formulas bit-for-bit.
```

**Auditing the numbers.** Every value on this page traces to
[`artifacts/sway_summary.csv`](artifacts/sway_summary.csv), and [`audit.py`](audit.py) re-checks the
metrics, the bit-exact match against the independent Prieto reimplementation, the internal consistency
(velocity = path/duration), the 95%-ellipse construct check, and the honestly noted scope (cross-tool
audit of a shipped op; machine precision; single-trial certification).
